blocks.x: In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

2026 has had the biggest summer in the short careers to date of real-life married couple Tom Holland and Zendaya. Not only did they both feature in Christopher Nolan's ambitious historical epic The Odyssey, which is currently the front-runner to take the Best Picture title and numerous other prizes at the Academy Awards next year, but they also both returned in the biggest film of the decade so far: Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The latest MCU blockbuster saw Holland and Zendaya return as Peter Parker and MJ, respectively, in a film that not only stole the hearts of long-time Spidey fans but also smashed all box office expectations. Of all its many box office achievements, the most impressive is becoming the highest-grossing film ever at the domestic box office, with a domestic haul that surpassed the $950 million mark. But Zendaya and Holland weren't the only actors to appear in both these huge 2026 blockbusters, as they did so alongside Jon Bernthal.

Bernthal's 2026 has been busy beyond these two hits, also starring in the surprise Netflix hit His & Hers, Marvel’s Special Presentation, The Punisher: One Last Kill, and the return of Christopher Storer’s The Bear. As the dust settles on a massive year for Bernthal, and he enjoys a well-earned break, his presence on the streaming charts is still impressive. At the time of writing, Bernthal's underrated 2025 spy thriller The Amateur is one of the ten most-streamed movies on Prime Video in the U.S., a list topped by Now You See Me: Now You Don’t, a heist threequel that features fellow Brand New Day alum Mark Ruffalo.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Coen Brothers Movie Would You Thrive In?
Lebowski · O Brother · Fargo · No Country

Nobody writes people like the Coen brothers. The decent ones. The talkers. The ones who stopped trying years ago. And the ones who can already see how bad this is going to get. Four films, four completely different ways of handling trouble. Eight questions decide which one you would actually walk out of.

A bag of money lands in your lap. What happens next?
Every Coen film starts roughly here. It never goes smoothly.

AI do not overthink it. Rent is paid, evening is free.
BI have a plan for this. It involves other people.
CI hand it in. Somebody is looking for this.
DI am gone before anyone knows I have it.

Somebody is being completely unreasonable with you. How does it go?
Coen dialogue is mostly people failing to understand each other.

AI let it go. It is not worth the energy.
BI talk. At length. Until they are on my side.
CI stay polite and repeat myself until they hear me.
DI stop talking. Talking has not been working.

What is your actual relationship with work?
Everyone in these films is either working far too hard or not at all.

AI have arranged things so I do as little as possible.
BI would rather chase one big idea than hold a steady job.
CI do it properly, including the boring parts.
DIt pays. I do not need it to mean anything.

Long drive, bad weather, nobody else on the road. How are you?
There is always a drive in these films. It is never a good drive.

AMusic on, in no hurry, perfectly content.
BTalking the whole way, whether anybody answers or not.
CBoth hands on the wheel, checking everyone is warm enough.
DQuiet, watching the mirrors.

You are offered a shortcut that is not quite legal.
This is the moment where the Coens find out who you really are.

ANo, but not on principle. It sounds like effort.
BYes, and I will make it sound like a great idea.
CNo. And I would probably say something about it.
DOnly if I am certain nobody finds out.

The plan has fallen apart completely. What is your move?
In a Coen film the plan always falls apart. That is the genre.

AOrder a drink and let things settle down.
BImprovise loudly and hope momentum carries it.
CStart again from the beginning and do it right.
DCut my losses and leave before it gets worse.

Which of these sounds most like something you would say?
Nobody writes a line quite like the Coens. Which one is yours?

AIt is really not that serious.
BTrust me, I have thought about this.
CI just think we could all be a bit kinder.
DThat was always going to happen.

How does your film end?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your movie.

ANothing is resolved and I am completely fine with it.
BA ridiculous piece of luck saves everybody.
CQuietly, at home, with somebody I love.
DSomebody older admits they no longer understand the world.

The Verdict Is In
Your Coen Film Is…

Four films, four completely different ways of handling money, trouble
and other people. This is the one you would survive, why it suits you, and what it would cost you to
be there.

You have quietly arranged your life so that very little can get
to you, and a surprising number of people find that infuriating. You would be completely at
home here.

The Dude is the only person in the film with no ambition, and the only one who comes out
the other side undamaged. That is not an accident.

You do not chase things. You let situations arrive and you deal with them at your own
pace, which is a genuine skill however lazy it looks.

This is a full crime plot happening around a man who mostly wants his rug back, and that
is exactly the energy you would bring to it.
Everything goes wrong. You abide. The film ends.

You talk your way through life and it works far more often than
it should. Give you a bad situation and an audience and you will find a way out of both at
once.

Everett never has a plan that survives contact with reality. He has something better,
which is the ability to keep talking until a new one turns up.

You are the optimist in the group, the one who makes a ridiculous idea sound reasonable
at two in the morning.

This is the warmest film the Coens have made. It is a chase, a comedy and a musical at
once, and nobody in it is quite beyond saving.
You would end up famous entirely by accident, and act like you planned it all along.

You would survive Fargo because you are the only kind of person
who does: patient, decent, and completely unimpressed by anybody trying to be clever.

Marge Gunderson solves the whole case by being polite, thorough and unhurried while
everybody around her panics. That is the entire argument of the film.

You do the boring parts of the job, which is precisely why you would notice the thing
everyone else walked straight past.

Fargo is about ordinary greed causing enormous damage, and about one person who simply
refuses to be corrupted by any of it.
You would go home at the end of it, have dinner, and sleep perfectly well.

You do not expect the world to be fair and you stopped being
surprised about it a long time ago. That clear-eyed quality is exactly what this film asks
for.

No Country is the Coens at their coldest: a film where being smart, fast and careful
might still not be anywhere near enough.

You plan for the worst, you keep your own counsel, and some part of you is already
working out the exit.

Llewelyn Moss is competent, prepared and resourceful, and the film is honest about
whether any of that is ever sufficient.

You would see it coming. Whether that helps is the one question the film refuses to
answer.
